description: I'm an independent researcher exploring AI, IoT and satellite applications. At AstroFurrow, I'll combine NASA Earth observations, local soil data, crop traits and farmer priorities to compare crop rotations as weather patterns shift.
summary: After the rice harvest in Tuku, Taiwan, when can a grower sow peanuts, and what can the field support in the following season? I built AstroFurrow Field School as a solo project for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Field Shift challenge. The website combines archived NASA weather data with example crop and soil profiles and adjustable field settings to compare two-season rotations. Five other missions explore different planting decisions. On India's Deccan Plateau, growers can compare fixed sowing with a rule based on completed monsoon rainfall records. In eastern Kenya, they can compare crop water shortfalls under pump and seasonal limits. In central Spain, they can move planting dates and test warmer conditions. In the Peruvian Andes, they can examine cold exposure and runoff from a hypothetical storm. In Brazil's Cerrado, they can follow soybean residue and soil water into the next season. Each mission shows what the model estimates and which conditions a grower can check locally before choosing a plan.
details:
In Tuku, Yunlin, the decision to plant peanuts after rice depends on how quickly the field drains and how much water the grower can set aside for the next crop. I built AstroFurrow Field School for Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data so growers and learners can explore how those conditions affect crop rotations. The browser-based prototype covers six example fields with different crops and constraints. The grower chooses what to plant.

How it works

Each mission compares three rotations over the same historical weather period. Users adjust the settings that matter in that location and inspect the results day by day. A daily water balance tracks rain, irrigation, runoff, drainage, soil evaporation and crop water use in two soil layers. The model carries remaining soil water and crop residue into the next season. NASA POWER supplies gridded GPM IMERG and MERRA-2 rainfall estimates. NASA SRTM elevations support the terrain view and a slope option in Peru. Quality-screened MODIS vegetation readings provide map context. Field and crop settings are illustrative, and the interface leaves unsupported results unavailable.

Tuku, Yunlin, Taiwan | What follows peanuts?

Users can move the peanut planting date and compare fallow, mustard cover or maize in the next season. When the second-season irrigation allowance drops from 100 mm to 0 mm, total simulated pumping across both seasons stays at 17.7 mm for the fallow plan. It falls from 32.1 to 16.4 mm for mustard and from 84.2 to 17.8 mm for maize. At the lower allowance, the model shows crop water shortfalls of 0.1 mm for mustard and 3.3 mm for maize. In a separate 72-hour exercise, both runs use a 10 mm pumping plan. At the end of the third day, simulated plant-available soil water is 50.3% of example capacity with archived IMERG rain and 48.9% with zero rain. The two runs fall on opposite sides of the exercise's 50% line.

Deccan Plateau, India | When has enough monsoon rain arrived?

The sowing rule tests a three-day rainfall total, then checks ten completed days for a dry spell longer than six days. With the archived IMERG rainfall and a 22 mm threshold, the rule schedules sorghum for 16 June 2024 UTC. The fixed-date sorghum plan starts on 20 June, and a seven-day equipment wait puts the rain-triggered millet plan on 23 June. The longest dry spell in the first fortnight is four days in each plan. A farm gauge, a workable sowing window and equipment availability would guide a new planting decision.

Eastern Kenya | What can a limited pump support?

In the example with a 5 mm/day pump limit and a 55 mm second-season allowance, maize followed by beans, sorghum followed by cowpeas, and millet followed by mung beans each use 121 mm of simulated pumping across both seasons. Their modelled crop water shortfalls are 131.9, 76.7 and 15.0 mm, respectively. The lesson lets users vary the starting water in the lower soil layer. When the irrigation water's salt concentration is unknown, the interface marks the amount of irrigation salt left in the soil as unknown and still shows water use. Starting soil salinity requires its own measurement.

Central Spain | Can a planting date reduce exposure to heat?

Users can shift the second planting date for cereal and pulse rotations. With dates and archived rain held fixed, adding a hypothetical 2°C raises the count of modelled hot days in the wheat-to-barley rotation from 21 to 31. FAO-56 reference evapotranspiration, an estimate of water demand for a standard reference surface, rises from 1,193.5 to 1,384.8 mm across the crop windows. Local temperature and the crop's growth stage would help a grower judge how those conditions matter in the field.

Peruvian Andes | Where do cold and storms matter on a slope?

The lesson lets users move the potato planting date to inspect cold exposure and compare slope assumptions in a storm scenario. For potatoes followed by fallow, a hypothetical 60 mm storm gives 14.6 mm of modelled runoff with either slope setting. The exposure score combines runoff, uncovered soil and slope. It is 7.33 with the slope derived from NASA SRTM elevation samples and 10.08 with the assumed slope. Cold pockets, actual flow paths, frost injury and erosion require separate field checks.

Brazilian Cerrado | What does the next crop inherit from soybeans?

Users compare leaving the field fallow, planting maize or planting millet after soybeans. In the soybean-to-maize replay, increasing the share of soybean harvest residue retained from 0% to 100% reduces the number of modelled days with less than 30% soil cover from 75 to zero. Simulated plant-available water at the start of season two rises from 143.1 to 149.6 mm. A grower can check how much cover remains after harvest and measure soil moisture at the next planting.

Teaching design and intended use

I designed the illustrated missions so a learner can change a setting, watch how water moves between soil layers and use the magnifier to look up an unfamiliar term. Maps and tables show the data behind the exercise. Growers and advisers can discuss what to measure before committing water or equipment time. In a Tuku pilot with grower consent, I would log the grower's usual practice, local rain, pumping and moisture in both soil layers. I would then run the same model with local inputs alone and with NASA data added. Field performance, water savings, crop yields, soil-carbon changes and student learning remain unmeasured.

Tools and credits

I developed the English Field School v1.7.0 with HTML, CSS, JavaScript and native SVG. I used Node.js for the static build and software tests. Local interface checks used Chrome. The separate offline Tuku calculator imports forecast files prepared with Python and ecCodes. The prototype runs on a standard computer with a web browser. I used ChatGPT for help with code, SVG graphics, English text, build tooling, tests and metadata. I included six conceptual story covers made with GPT Image, each with visible generation credits. The local seven-slide English presentation shows the six missions and walks through the Tuku tests.
